scenes.heading: Partitioning at Scale
scenes.subheading: How Spark and query engines split work
scenes.narration: In distributed engines like Spark, partitioning determines how data is divided into parallel units of work, and it is the single biggest lever on job performance.

scenes.heading: Partitioning that matters
bullets: Input partitions set the initial parallelism
Skew leaves a few tasks running long
scenes.narration: Input partitions come from how files are split and set your initial parallelism. Shuffle partitions control how many tasks run after a wide operation like a join or aggregation. Partition pruning lets the engine skip entire folders or files when a filter matches the partition column, saving huge amounts of I O. And data skew, where a few keys carry most of the rows, leaves a handful of straggler tasks running long after the rest finish.

scenes.heading: Too few vs too many partitions

left.label: Too few
points: Long tail on a single core

scenes.narration: With too few partitions the cluster sits idle because there is not enough parallel work, individual tasks grow large and spill to disk, and one oversized task can dominate the runtime. With too many partitions the scheduler spends more time managing tiny tasks than doing useful work, and writing them out produces the small-file problem that slows later reads. The goal is enough partitions to keep every core busy without drowning in overhead, often a few times the total core count.

scenes.heading: Repartition and handle skew
scenes.code:
# Increase shuffle parallelism for a large join
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 400)

# Repartition by the join key to co-locate rows
sales = sales.repartition(400, "customer_id")

# Salting a skewed key to spread hot values
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
sales = sales.withColumn(
    "salt", (F.rand() * 10).cast("int")
).withColumn("skey", F.concat_ws("_", "customer_id", "salt"))
scenes.narration: Here we first raise the shuffle partition count so a large join spreads across four hundred tasks instead of the default. We repartition the sales data by the join key so matching rows land together and reduce shuffle. Then we tackle skew by salting the hot key, appending a random bucket so a single dominant customer id is split into ten sub-keys. The join then runs against the salted key and no single task is overwhelmed.

scenes.heading: How a shuffle executes
steps: Map tasks read and filter input
scenes.narration: During a wide transformation the map tasks read and filter their input partitions. Each output row is hashed by the partitioning key to decide which reduce partition it belongs to, and the results are written to local shuffle files. The reduce tasks then fetch across the network only the shuffle blocks belonging to their partition. Finally each reduce task performs the join or aggregation on the rows it received.

scenes.heading: Avoiding shuffle when you can
bullets: Broadcast small tables to skip the shuffle
Co-partition datasets on the join key
Filter and project before the shuffle
scenes.narration: The cheapest shuffle is the one you avoid. Broadcasting a small table to every executor lets a join happen locally with no shuffle at all. Co-partitioning two datasets on the same join key up front means the engine can join them without re-exchanging data. Filtering and projecting columns before a wide operation shrinks how much data must move. And adaptive query execution can dynamically coalesce shuffle partitions at runtime, merging tiny ones so you avoid the overhead of too many small tasks.

scenes.text: Tune partition counts to your cluster, prune aggressively, and salt skewed keys so parallelism stays balanced end to end.
scenes.narration: Right-size your partition counts to the cluster, prune partitions aggressively with well-placed filters, and salt skewed keys so that parallelism stays balanced and no single task becomes the bottleneck.
